11	The JusPrin v2 Figma file is `https://www.figma.com/design/jo9J1sK9ZZ0vxncWnSp0vH/JusPrin-v2` (Kenneth signs the built-in browser in on request; it is not signed in by default). No Figma MCP connector was attached as of 2026-10-02, and the page exposes no `figma` plugin global to scripts.
12	
13	Exact numbers come from Figma's own export, not from screenshots:
14	
15	1. In the Layers panel, right-click the frame (use `find` for the layer name, then right-click its ref).
16	2. Copy/Paste as → Copy as code → **CSS (all layers)**. The menu rows are DOM, so `find` + hover/click by ref works.
17	3. Read it back with `Get-Clipboard -Raw` in PowerShell. One frame is about 45 KB: every layer's size, padding, gap, fill, border, radius, and its text style name ("Label Bold", "Metadata Bold", …), which maps one-to-one onto `typography.roles` in `resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json`.
18

20	
21	Fill colors come out as hex; match them to semantic tokens by value. A hex with no token (the left pane's `#E8F5EE` "Sliced" chip) is a token to add, with a guard, before any code uses it.

Yes, I have what I need to start. I checked the handoff against the Figma file and the repo, and the one thing you'll need to confirm is the build/test setup, which I haven't checked yet.

**What I confirmed**
- **Figma:** the built-in browser is signed in to JusPrin v2. The "Plates & Project Pane" page lists every frame the handoff names: 26a, 26b, 26c1, 26c2, 26d1, 26d2, 26e1–e4, 26f and 26h. Frame 26g isn't in the Layers panel, which fits it being out of scope. I can pull exact geometry and type roles from these frames using the "Copy as code → CSS (all layers)" method in my notes.
- **Repo:** all the docs and files the handoff points to exist, including `design-system.md`, `fork-stewardship.md`, `design-tokens.json`, `ShellController`, `StatusRow`, `Workspace.hpp`, `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter`, `ProjectState.hpp`, `ManufacturingHistory`, `ProjectStateDocument`, `CanvasPresentationController` and `ViewportToolStrip`.
- **Spec:** the behavior, data-ownership and acceptance sections are specific enough to build from.

**Limits I already know about**
- **Wording:** Figma's CSS export doesn't include text content. For copy such as menu labels and the "N won't print" phrasing, I'll have to zoom the canvas onto each layer and read it.
- **Missing tokens:** colors like the `#E8F5EE` "Sliced" chip have no token yet. Per the design-system rules, I add the token and a guard before any code uses it.
- **Read-model gaps:** the handoff lists six gaps in the workspace snapshot (per-instance IDs and off-plate instances, named child rows, a shared command surface, customization facts, mesh-problem status, attachment open paths). Those are the first step of the work, with tests, so I'll write code as well as read it.
- **Verification:** I can verify on Windows. The macOS/Linux and 150%/200% scaling checks need other machines or settings.

**Before I start, I'd like you to confirm**
1. Should I work on this branch (`claude/open-figma-browser-86ed07`)? It is based on `jusprin-newui` work, but it's a worktree named for opening Figma.
2. Is it OK to leave the handoff file untracked, as the file itself says?
3. Do you want me to build and run it here, using your own build tree and an isolated `--datadir`? The build machine has no debugger and the RDP session has to stay connected for visual checks.

If yes to all three, I'll start with step 1 of the suggested order: the read-model tests for plate membership, per-copy printability, folded summaries, off-plate instances and hierarchy.
yes to all three, go ahead

4	
5	Read these documents in order:
6	
7	1. [Product definition](product-definition.md) — the human/agent boundary, required product surfaces, workflow, and visibility rules.
8	2. [Production architecture](architecture.md) — the selected native/WebView architecture, ownership rules, component boundaries, and implementation sequence.
9	3. [Engineering and verification method](engineering-method.md) — how to assess risk and what evidence is required before calling a feature complete.
10	4. [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) — known Orca behaviors, lifecycle traps, event and history constraints, and testing lessons.
11	5. [Fork stewardship](fork-stewardship.md) — required before changing any OrcaSlicer-owned file: where a seam belongs, why additive beats rewritten, how to leave a conflict that resolves correctly, and what evidence a change must record.
12	6. [Design system](design-system.md) — brand behavior, semantic UI tokens, typography, spacing, accessibility, and asset rules.
13	7. [POC reference](poc-reference.md) — exact pointers to the spike-only documents, code, commits, logs, screenshots, and generated brand artifacts left on `jusprin-v2-poc`.
14	8. [Tool extension guide](mcp-tool-extension-guide.md) — shared Agent/MCP contracts, process-settings workflow, approval and verification requirements.

18	
19	## Governing decisions
20	
21	- JusPrin is an AI-piloted 3D-printing product built on OrcaSlicer, not a replacement slicing engine.
22	- OrcaSlicer's C++ model, slicing pipeline, viewport, geometry operations, project serialization, and undo stack remain authoritative.
23	- The production application stays native C++/wxWidgets/OpenGL. The Agent conversation uses a local React/TypeScript application inside `wxWebView`.
24	- JavaScript renders state and submits typed commands; it never owns editable Orca project state.
25	- When logic could live in either C++ or a React page, it goes in the page unless there is a strong reason for C++: it touches Orca state, enforces a limit or boundary the app must guarantee, has to work without a page, or needs a thread or lifetime the page lacks. See [Where logic goes](architecture.md#where-logic-goes-the-page-first).
26	- Product policy lives in fork-owned files. OrcaSlicer-owned files receive only small, product-neutral, additive seams — every line changed there is a line this fork re-resolves at every rebase.
27	- The user owns physical facts, object meaning, desired outcomes, privacy and legal decisions, and authorization of consequential physical actions.
28	- The production branch must not import experimental POC behavior merely because it demonstrated feasibility. Use the POC as evidence and reimplement through stable production boundaries.
29	
30	## Source lineage

32	`jusprin-newui` and `jusprin-v2-poc` share base commit `8500fcdcca` (`v2.4.2`). The POC reference is pinned to final POC commit `9bba835b92`, so future changes to branch names do not make the historical evidence ambiguous.

1	# JusPrin engineering and verification method
2	
3	**Status:** Required planning, implementation, and release-verification method for `jusprin-newui`.
4	
5	JusPrin is changing the presentation of a mature manufacturing application. The main engineering risk is not whether common UI technology can work; it is whether new presentation code bypasses, duplicates, or destabilizes authoritative Orca behavior.
6	
7	## Risk vocabulary
8	
9	Risk means residual, evidence-backed uncertainty that could materially affect architecture, correctness, delivery, regressions, or a physical print after mature precedent has been considered.
10	
11	Keep these categories separate:
12	
13	- **Feasibility:** whether a technical boundary can work at all.
14	- **Integration:** whether proven components can be connected without unsafe ownership or duplicated behavior.
15	- **Product behavior:** uncertainty about what the feature must do.
16	- **Delivery effort:** understood implementation work, even when substantial.
17	- **Regression exposure:** risk of disturbing mature Orca behavior.
18	- **Platform QA:** evidence required for a particular OS, WebView backend, display stack, input method, or DPI.
19	
20	A known bug, untested platform, or inconvenient implementation detail is not automatically an architecture risk.
21	
22	## Required assessment process
23	
24	Before adding a spike or assigning a risk label:
25	
26	1. Define the user-visible requirement without assuming an implementation or cause.
27	2. Classify the underlying technical capability.
28	3. Search for mature precedent in the current Orca code, Orca history and forks, comparable slicers, mature same-stack applications, and finally framework documentation.
29	4. State what the precedent proves and where it differs.
30	5. Isolate only the unproven delta.
31	6. Record the plausible failure, evidence for likelihood, consequence, blast radius, reversibility, and cheapest resolving evidence.
32	7. Choose code inspection, a focused test, an integration prototype, platform validation, or a feasibility spike according to the uncertainty.
33	
34	A new visual arrangement is not necessarily a new technical capability. Spike only consequential uncertainty that mature code and focused tests cannot answer.
35	
36	## Current evidence ledger
37	
38	| Requirement | Established evidence | Remaining production delta | Current classification |
39	|---|---|---|---|
40	| Native shell | Orca already composes native panels and `GLCanvas3D`; the exact native/WebView boundary ran on macOS and Linux/X11 | Production shell behavior and remaining platform/input coverage | Very low feasibility; integration and platform QA remain |
41	| Agent pane and bridge | Orca has local/remote WebViews, script handlers, and native/JS communication | Versioned schema, recovery, focus rules, authentication, production UI | Low architecture risk |
42	| Thin object/plate pane | `GUI_ObjectList`, `ObjectDataViewModel`, `Plater`, and `PartPlate` contain the behavior | A small behavior-oriented API without copied presentation logic | Low feasibility; medium integration |
43	| Canvas action strip | Orca projects selection bounds and activates gizmos | Product positioning rules and reusable controller | Low |
44	| Exact transform entry | `GizmoObjectManipulation` applies values and snapshots | Separate behavior from old ImGui presentation | Low feasibility; medium coupling |
45	| Semantic facet annotations | Existing painter tools prove picking, painting, visualization, copying, undo, and persistence | Arbitrary label schema and lifecycle, especially topology changes | Low feasibility; medium data-model risk |
46	| Gizmo rollout | Existing tools share selection, rendering, and history infrastructure | Different interaction families need distinct adapters | Medium delivery/regression; low architecture |
47	| Slicing, picking, history, Preview | Mature production subsystems retained unchanged | Ensure presentation never bypasses them | Low when boundary is enforced |
48	
49	Update this ledger when evidence changes. Do not carry an old risk label forward without checking current code and results.
50	
51	## Test strategy
52	
53	### Regression baselines and failure classification
54	
55	Run the closest existing test and the broadest practical baseline before changing
56	an upstream-owned behavior. Record pre-existing failures by exact test name and
57	failure mode so later runs can distinguish a regression from inherited state.
58	
59	When a broad suite fails, rerun the exact case independently before assigning a
60	cause. Record repeatable failures as regressions until disproved; record a
61	one-time timeout, deadlock, or infrastructure failure separately with the
62	isolated rerun result. A green focused suite does not erase a new repeatable
63	broad-suite failure.
64	
65	### Contract tests
66	
67	Test strong IDs, invalid/missing/stale identifiers, command errors, subscription lifetime, event coalescing, revision behavior, and fake-workspace history without linking the GUI. Test both successful and unsuccessful commands, and assert that reported results agree with authoritative state.
68	
69	### Real-adapter application tests
70	
71	A fake cannot validate `Plater`, `GLCanvas3D`, plate membership, `GUI_ObjectList` dependencies, event ordering, or Orca's undo stack. Add an application-level harness that loads deterministic project fixtures and covers:
72	
73	- project-ready signaling rather than fixed event-loop delays;
74	- a dedicated application name and bundle identity so UI automation cannot target another Orca build;
75	- an isolated temporary configuration and repository-owned fixture;
76	- deterministic on-bed object placement, active tab, selection, and camera-visible state before reporting readiness;
77	- object and viewport selection in both directions;
78	- rename, duplicate, remove, plate switch, import, undo, and redo;
79	- committed native transform and exact-value transform;
80	- callback snapshots at the advertised revision;
81	- subscriber destruction;
82	- project replacement and session-ID invalidation;
83	- operations initiated outside the adapter.
84	
85	The POC self-test is evidence and test-design input, not a production harness: its STL setup could not reproduce rename undo, and it intentionally terminated through `std::_Exit`.
86	
87	### Shell end-to-end tests
88	
89	Run the complete native application with a deterministic multi-plate project. Verify the visible real canvas, camera controls, selection, native gizmos, Slice, Check print, return to Prepare, undo/redo, object pane synchronization, Agent pane persistence, resize, maximize/restore, and the unchanged legacy layout when testing a compatibility mode.
90	
91	Visual appearance alone is insufficient. Validate state from authoritative callbacks and pair visibility claims with screenshots or rendered evidence.
92	
93	Use the harness to establish deterministic application state; use UI automation
94	for real pointer, keyboard, focus, and rendering checks rather than for fragile
95	startup setup. For canvas policy, inventory every overlay surface and verify
96	rendering and hit-testing separately. Compare a stock window with the product
97	policy, then exercise selection, orbit, pan, zoom, active gizmo input, slicing,
98	Preview, and restoration of the prior presentation state.
99	
100	### Printer tests without hardware
101	
102	Bambu paths (printer-menu Idle / Printing / Offline, Select Machine, print job)
103	are exercised by an in-process fake that substitutes for the Bambu printer
104	agent while a real Bambu Lab **system** preset stays selected. How to turn it
105	on, the JSON control file, isolated-instance rules for agents, and acceptance
106	checks: [Fake Bambu README](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md).
107	
108	The Klipper/Moonraker network simulator lives on `jusprin-newui-fakeprinter`
109	under `tests/printer_sim/` and covers print-host paths. Do not add a fake
110	Bambu network layer (MQTT/FTPS/discovery) without an explicit request.
111	
112	### Platform matrix
113	
114	Before release completion, cover:
115	
116	- Windows with WebView2;
117	- macOS with WKWebView;
118	- Linux/X11 and supported Wayland configurations with WebKitGTK;
119	- supported CPU architectures and a physical GPU where applicable;
120	- 100%, 150%, and 200% scaling or equivalent platform DPI settings;
121	- light and dark mode;
122	- keyboard focus, global shortcuts, clipboard, text selection, and IME composition;
123	- WebView startup, local resource loading, reload, and recovery;
124	- streaming scroll anchoring while orbiting and resizing;
125	- idle and streaming CPU/memory observations.
126	
127	Classify localized CSS, focus, packaging, or backend problems as platform defects unless evidence shows they require a different architecture.
128	
129	### Software GL on Windows machines without a GPU
130	
131	A Windows machine with no graphics driver reports system GL 1.1, so the launcher
132	(`src/OrcaSlicer_app_msvc.cpp`) loads `<exe dir>\mesa\opengl32.dll` instead.
133	Nothing in CMake or this repository supplies that file or what it depends on, so
134	provision every freshly configured build tree with
135	`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/windows-gl/provision-mesa-windows.ps1`.
136	Placement is not interchangeable:
137	
138	| file | goes | because |
139	| --- | --- | --- |
140	| `opengl32.dll` | `mesa\` subfolder | the launcher loads it by that path; beside the executable it shadows the system GL and the app dies at launch |
141	| `opengl32.dll` again | beside each `*_harness.exe` | a harness links the app in and has no launcher, so only a copy beside it replaces the system GL 1.1 |
142	| `libgallium_wgl.dll` | beside the executable | the `opengl32.dll` stub imports it, and Windows resolves imports against the process directory |
143	| `dxil.dll` | beside the executable | Mesa's `d3d12` driver signs translated shaders with it; Windows Server does not ship it, Windows SDKs carry it under `Redist\D3D\x64` |
144	
145	Each gap has its own silent signature:
146	
147	- **No `libgallium_wgl.dll`:** GL falls back to 1.1, the log has `glcontext not ready, postpone init` and no `got opengl version` line, and the canvas stays black for the whole session — the retry after a postponed init exists only on Linux.
148	- **No `opengl32.dll` beside a harness:** the same GL 1.1 signature, in the harness only. The canvas never builds its volumes, so `Plater::select_object` returns false after `load_files`, and the workspace harness then crashed opening a paint gizmo with nothing selected (`0xC0000005`).
149	- **No `dxil.dll`:** GL initializes through `d3d12`, then the process exits with `0x80070057` on the first canvas draw, with no log line, no dialog, and no event-log entry. `slow_bootup` only moves this crash from startup to the first canvas paint.
150	
151	Confirm what actually loaded from the process's module list rather than from
152	file presence. The log names the live driver: `4.6 … llvmpipe` is Mesa's software
153	rasterizer, `4.2 … D3D12 (Microsoft Basic Render Driver)` is Mesa's `d3d12`
154	driver on WARP. A fully provisioned tree renders under both;
155	`GALLIUM_DRIVER=llvmpipe` selects the former.
156	
157	## Implementation evidence record
158	
159	For every production area, record:
160	
161	- product requirement and underlying technical nature;
162	- current Orca command owner, snapshot location, and event source;
163	- mature precedents and what each proves;
164	- remaining delta and risk category;
165	- production and upstream-owned files touched;
166	- verification command and exit condition;
167	- platforms exercised and gaps remaining;
168	- regression checks for the original Orca path;
169	- any behavior that could not be tested and why.
170	
171	## Rebase evidence
172	
173	The rules for changing upstream-owned files are in [fork stewardship](fork-stewardship.md). This section states only what a change must produce as evidence.
174	
175	A change that touches an upstream-owned file is not finished until the handback or pull request records three things:
176	
177	1. **The rebase simulation and its result**, run against current upstream with both endpoint commits named. For each conflicted file, state whether the natural resolution is correct or lossy. A lossy resolution is a defect to fix before the change lands, not a note for the person who rebases.
178	2. **Every upstream line deleted or rewritten**, with where the logic went and why an additive form was not possible.
179	3. **What the fork now owns** — product policy, a small neutral seam, or upstream behavior. The third needs an explicit justification.
180	
181	An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It never proves that a future rebase will merge, and never proves that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the contract tests, the full native build, the multi-plate Prepare/Check workflow, native gizmo input, and the original-Orca regression checks.
182	
183	The incidents that produced these rules are in [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md). Historical logs and spike procedures are in [POC reference](poc-reference.md).
184

1	# JusPrin design system
2	
3	**Status:** Canonical product and brand guidance for `jusprin-newui`.
4	
5	JusPrin should make advanced 3D printing feel immediate: a confident path from model to machine that removes detours without hiding control. The product should feel focused, assured, inventive, and approachable. Its voice is direct, capable, and optimistic—never cute, cryptic, or over-engineered.
6	
7	The original JusPrin logo was supplied by the user and restored from repository revision `6eecb78b19`. The purple gradient endpoints were verified from the source SVG. Positioning language in the POC brand kit is proposed product direction, not an externally sourced market claim.
8	
9	## Brand behavior
10	
11	- **Focused:** every element earns its place.
12	- **Assured:** guidance is calm and actions are decisive.
13	- **Inventive:** the product is technical without being intimidating.
14	- **Approachable:** use plain language instead of slicer jargon where possible.
15	- Make the next action obvious. Brand behavior should feel as focused as the visual system.
16	
17	The logo suggests an end-to-end journey through its orbit, precision and momentum through the crossing diagonals, flexible control through the open circle, and technical confidence softened by warmth through the purple gradient.
18	
19	Write the name exactly as **JusPrin**: capital J and P, no space, never all caps in body copy. Use surrounding text color for the name in ordinary copy; do not force a gradient into small text.
20	
21	## Logo use
22	
23	The primary expressions are the horizontal lockup, the compact product mark, and the text wordmark. Use the compact mark for application icons and small product contexts.
24	
25	- Clear space: at least one quarter of the mark width on every side.
26	- Minimum digital mark: 24 px.
27	- Minimum digital horizontal lockup: 120 px.
28	- Minimum printed mark: 8 mm.
29	- Minimum printed lockup: 32 mm.
30	- Below these sizes, use the mark alone and verify that the orbit arcs remain distinct.
31	
32	Always use the original artwork, preserve its aspect ratio and components, maintain clear space, and place it on White, Mist, Ink, or another quiet solid field. Do not stretch, rotate, redraw, arbitrarily recolor, outline, shadow, separate, or place it directly over visual noise. Monochrome is allowed only when required. If the center crossing or orbit loses clarity, increase size, contrast, or space.
33	
34	## Brand palette
35	
36	| Name | Value | Use |
37	|---|---:|---|
38	| Orbit | `#3A2D64` | Primary brand color and decisive light-mode action |
39	| Violet | `#6F4F84` | Secondary brand color, headings, and essential boundaries |
40	| Bloom | `#CE84B7` | Expressive accent and dark-mode primary action |
41	| Ink | `#17131F` | Primary text and dark canvas |
42	| Mist | `#F6F2F7` | Soft canvas and grouped surfaces |
43	| Trace | `#E8DFEB` | Light dividers and quiet structure |
44	| White | `#FFFFFF` | Primary light canvas |
45	| Success | `#2D6A55` | Light success state |
46	| Danger | `#B44757` | Light error or destructive state |
47	| Warning | `#D49A2A` | Light warning state |
48	
49	The signature gradient runs from Orbit to Bloom. Reserve it for the original logo, splash, onboarding, and rare hero moments. Do not use it as ordinary product chrome.
50	
51	Product code must resolve colors through semantic tokens in `resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json`; raw palette values are not a component API.
52	
53	## Semantic color behavior
54	
55	Dark mode is a semantic remapping, not a visual inversion. Preserve hierarchy, density, and geometry while choosing the dark value for the same named intent.
56	
57	Core mappings include:
58	
59	| Token | Light | Dark | Purpose |
60	|---|---:|---:|---|
61	| `surface.canvas` | `#FFFFFF` | `#17131F` | Main application background |
62	| `surface.subtle` | `#F6F2F7` | `#211B2A` | Sidebars and grouped settings |
63	| `surface.raised` | `#FFFFFF` | `#2B2336` | Dialogs, menus, elevated panels |
64	| `text.primary` | `#17131F` | `#F6F2F7` | Headings, values, body copy |
65	| `text.secondary` | `#5F5767` | `#CFC5D3` | Descriptions and secondary labels |
66	| `border.subtle` | `#E8DFEB` | `#4B3E57` | Dividers and quiet structure |
67	| `border.strong` | `#6F4F84` | `#7D6A8D` | Focus and essential boundaries |
68	| `action.primary` | `#3A2D64` | `#CE84B7` | Decisive primary action |
69	| `action.primary.hover` | `#4B3A77` | `#D99AC5` | Pointer hover |
70	| `action.primary.pressed` | `#2B214F` | `#B76CA0` | Pressed or active state |
71	
72	The JSON token file is authoritative and contains the complete action, status, selected-surface, disabled, text, and component values.
73	
74	## Typography
75	
76	Product UI uses fonts already shipped by OrcaSlicer:
77	
78	- HarmonyOS Sans SC Regular for body and controls.
79	- HarmonyOS Sans SC Bold for hierarchy and actions.
80	- NanumGothic for Korean and Sarabun for Thai where the existing application requires them.
81	- The system GUI font as fallback.
82	- The system monospace font only for code: API keys, file paths, commands, config text, and IDs such as hashes. Never for names, words, or measurements.
83	
84	HarmonyOS Sans SC draws every digit at the same width, so times, percentages,
85	and other values that change in place do not shift in the UI face; they do
86	not need the monospace one. The native shell has no monospace text.
87	
88	Never require Menlo or another platform-specific face. The broader marketing brand kit used Avenir Next for display and marketing; that is not the cross-platform product UI requirement.
89	
90	| Role | Size/line height in DIP | Weight |
91	|---|---:|---|
92	| Page title | 24/30 | Bold |
93	| Section | 18/24 | Bold |
94	| Body and control | 14/20 | Regular |
95	| Body bold | 14/20 | Bold |
96	| Body small | 13/18 | Regular |
97	| Body small bold | 13/18 | Bold |
98	| Label | 12/16 | Regular |
99	| Label bold | 12/16 | Bold |
100	| Dense metadata | 10/14 | Regular |
101	| Dense metadata bold | 10/14 | Bold |
102	| Code (system monospace) | 12/16 | Regular |
103	
104	The bold pairs exist for emphasis inside a run of the same size (a primary
105	action beside secondary ones, the current row of a menu, a chip's name beside
106	its detail). Code is a single role, `typography.code`, whatever size the
107	text around it is.
108	
109	## Layout and geometry
110	
111	Design for a dense, native, high-DPI desktop application on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Use device-independent pixels (DIP), not physical pixels. Verify 100%, 150%, and 200% scaling.
112	
113	- Spacing scale: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, and 48 DIP.
114	- Standard control radius: 4 DIP, matching OrcaSlicer's own controls.
115	- Compact or branded action radius: 8 DIP.
116	- Container radius: 8 DIP, for grouped panels and cards, matching OrcaSlicer's `StaticBox` default.
117	- Window action and large-dialog radius: 12 DIP.
118	- Capsule radius: `pill`, for status chips and progress tracks whose shape is
119	  the full height. Menu rows sit inset 4 DIP inside the popover and carry the
120	  standard radius, so a hovered row reads as a control inside the panel
121	  rather than a stripe across it.
122	- Reserve 16–24 DIP radii for onboarding and marketing, not the main application shell.
123	
124	Avoid web-only assumptions such as oversized controls, blur-heavy or glass surfaces, fixed physical pixels, and platform-specific fonts.
125	
126	## Components and states
127	
128	Use the existing native component density and established SVG icon library. Functional clarity comes before logo-derived decoration.
129	
130	- Functional icons: 16, 20, or 24 DIP, with PNG fallback when the platform path requires it.
131	- Orbit motif: progress, connection, or active workflow; verify stroke clarity at output size.
132	- Directional accent: at most one diagonal for momentum; avoid decorative competing angles.
133	- Compact button: 8×3 DIP padding, 8 DIP radius, dense metadata text.
134	- Window button: minimum 58×24 DIP, 12 DIP radius, 12 DIP text.
135	- Choice control: minimum 100×32 DIP, 12×8 DIP padding, 4 DIP radius.
136	- Parameter control: 120×26 DIP, 4 DIP radius, 14 DIP text.
137	- Icon button: 26×26 DIP, 16 DIP icon, 4 DIP radius.
138	- Expanded button: at least 32 DIP high, 12×8 DIP padding, 4 DIP radius.
139	- Agent-pane divider: transparent 8 DIP pointer target with a centered 2 DIP line; the line changes from subtle to strong on hover and to the primary action color while dragging.
140	- Agent-pane width: minimum 320 DIP; its maximum follows the window width while preserving at least 320 DIP for the workspace.
141	- Printer setup, connecting, printer settings, and filament settings help use the same temporary conversation layer over the originating workspace. The underlying Home, Prepare, or Preview screen stays selected and constructed so Back returns to it. The conversation keeps the centered content width from `component.printerSetup.contentWidth` and the existing task header controls; manual settings remain available from that header. The saved project Agent pane remains a separate persistent conversation.
142	- Agent-pane collapse: a 26 DIP icon button in the header, left of the overflow button, whose glyph fills its right-hand column while the pane is open and empties it while the pane is closed. Double-clicking the divider closes the pane. Dragging it does not: a drag only sizes the pane and stops at its 320 DIP minimum, so aiming for a narrow pane never takes the conversation off the screen. There is no keyboard shortcut, no animation, and no automatic reopening; the pane is hidden, never destroyed, so its conversation survives. Reopening restores the width it last held.
143	
144	Every interactive component must define normal, hover, pressed, disabled, focused, success, warning, and error states where relevant. Status must combine color with an icon and plain-language label.
145	
146	## Accessibility
147	
148	- Normal text requires at least 4.5:1 contrast; 3:1 is allowed only for large text.
149	- Essential control boundaries and state indicators require 3:1.
150	- Keyboard focus uses a visible 2 DIP ring and may not rely on a fill-color change alone.
151	- Orbit on White measures 12.07:1 in the source design system.
152	- Bloom on Ink measures 6.62:1.
153	- Light secondary text measures 6.89:1 on White.
154	- Dark secondary text measures 10.95:1 on Ink.
155	
156	## Writing UI code
157	
158	Rules for anyone, human or agent, adding or changing a JusPrin surface. They
159	exist because every value that is typed by hand drifts from Figma and from
160	the other side of the app within weeks; today's guards catch most of it, but
161	only if the code goes through the token file in the first place.
162	
163	1. **Never type a color, radius, font, or control size.** Every one comes
164	   from `resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json`. Native code reads it
165	   through `ShellTheme`: `palette(dark)` for color, `metrics()` for radii,
166	   spacing, and per-component sizes, `font(role)` for type. A stock
167	   `wxStaticText`, `wxTextCtrl`, or OrcaSlicer `Button` is
168	   dressed through `Shell/ShellRecipes.hpp`, never by calling its setters
169	   with literals. The Agent page uses only `var(--…)`: `--<group>-<name>` for
170	   color, `--radius-<name>`, `--font-<role>`, `--font-code`, and
171	   `--button-<recipe>-padding`.
172	2. **If the value you need has no token, add the token first.** Put it in
173	   the JSON, extend the guard in `tests/brand/test_brand_tokens.cpp` so a
174	   later edit cannot silently move it, then read it from code. Do not write
175	   the number "for now": the guards cannot see a literal that is already
176	   there, and the next reader cannot tell a decision from an accident. A
177	   value that exists in Figma but not in the roles or scales is a design
178	   decision to raise, not a reason to type it.
179	3. **Layout spacing may stay literal, on the scale.** Padding between
180	   regions, gaps, and margins use 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, or 48 DIP.
181	   Control padding is not layout spacing; it comes from a button recipe.
182	4. **Pick the nearest role, never a bespoke size.** The roles are the whole
183	   type system. Bold at a body or label size is a role of its own; if a
184	   surface seems to need a size that no role has, see rule 2.
185	5. **Read the code on `jusprin-newui`, not old commit messages or Figma,
186	   when they disagree.** The header's chip and menu dimensions were once
187	   changed to match Figma and reverted because they looked worse; the
188	   token file records what stayed.
189	6. **Run the guards before calling UI work done:** `brand_tokens_tests`,
190	   `shell_theme_tests`, and `npm test` in `AgentUI`. Then look at the surface
191	   in the running app; the guards prove the code went through the tokens,
192	   not that the result looks right.
193	7. **Upstream files are off limits for style.** OrcaSlicer's own screens are
194	   retinted through the hooks `BrandPalette.cpp` installs and nothing else;
195	   see [Fork stewardship](fork-stewardship.md). Their radii and fonts stay
196	   OrcaSlicer's until the surface is replaced.
197	
198	## Runtime application in the native app
199	
200	The token file is applied to the running application in three layers. All
201	three read `resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json`; none of them carries a
202	color literal of its own, and the whole layer touches OrcaSlicer code in only
203	three small, additive seams plus one attachment point.
204	
205	1. **Fork-owned surfaces** (`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Shell/*`, the React Agent
206	   page) resolve every style through the token file, not only color.
207	   - Native: `ShellTheme` exposes `palette(dark)` for color, `metrics()` for
208	     the radius and spacing scales and the per-component sizes, `font(role)`
209	     for the type roles above. It is loaded once, by `Brand/BrandPalette.cpp`, and passed
210	     by reference into every shell widget. Widgets that paint themselves read
211	     it directly; a stock `wxStaticText`, `wxTextCtrl`, or OrcaSlicer `Button`
212	     is dressed through the three functions in `Shell/ShellRecipes.hpp`, so no
213	     fork-owned C++ file names an OrcaSlicer font preset or writes a radius as
214	     a number. `tests/jusprin/test_shell_theme.cpp` checks the parse and the
215	     fonts.
216	   - Web: `AgentUI/src/tokens.ts` writes the semantic colors as
217	     `--<group>-<name>` on every appearance change, and once at startup the
218	     radii as `--radius-<name>` and each type role as a complete `font`
219	     shorthand, `--font-<role>` in the UI face, plus `--font-code` for the one
220	     monospace role. The stylesheet may only say `var(--…)` for color, radius,
221	     and type; `AgentUI/src/styles.test.ts` reads the stylesheet from disk and
222	     fails on any literal, and on any spacing value off the scale.
223	   - Canvas: the Prepare canvas's tool strip (`Canvas/ViewportToolStrip`)
224	     paints with ImGui inside the GL frame, from the same `ShellTheme`. Its
225	     icons are the `currentColor` SVGs in `resources/jusprin/ui/icons`,
226	     rasterized white and tinted with the token colour. ImGui 1.83 has no
227	     shadow primitive, so `elevation.medium` is approximated with stacked
228	     translucent rounded rectangles.
229	2. **Retained OrcaSlicer surfaces** are retinted through the color tables
230	   OrcaSlicer already routes its colors through, installed once per appearance
231	   mode by `JusPrin/Brand/BrandPalette.cpp` from the end of
232	   `GUI_App::init_label_colours`:
233	   - `StateColor::SetColorOverrides` maps OrcaSlicer's brand and surface
234	     literals (teal family, grays, whites, text grays) to semantic tokens before
235	     OrcaSlicer's own dark-mode remap runs. Every widget built on `StateColor`
236	     switches at once.
237	   - `BitmapCache::SetColorReplaces` rewrites the teal in the SVG icon set to
238	     the action color at load time, and the monochrome brand mark to the text
239	     color.
240	   - The canvas selection is OrcaSlicer's own, unretinted: its silhouette
241	     outline, which OrcaSlicer ships switched off and the shell switches on
242	     while it is installed, plus its white corner brackets. The brackets were
243	     briefly given the primary action color; on the dark build plate that
244	     measured 1.29:1 in light mode against white's 9:1, and with the outline
245	     carrying the selection the override was dropped on 2026-09-21, which
246	     left `Selection` untouched by the fork again.
247	   - The ImGui panels, the canvas selection rectangle, and the About dialog
248	     are left alone in source: those surfaces are slated to be hidden or
249	     replaced, so editing them would be divergence with no lasting value.
250	   - The mapping table in `BrandPalette.cpp` is the reviewed teal-to-purple
251	     decision. Extend it there; never add a purple literal to an OrcaSlicer file.
252	   - Widgets that paint the teal without going through `StateColor` (hyperlinks,
253	     the settings tab underline, notification accents, Bambu-only dialogs) are
254	     deliberately left teal; the cost of editing them in busy upstream files
255	     outweighs surfaces JusPrin rarely or never shows.
256	3. **Identity** comes from two data-only mechanisms:
257	   - `resources/jusprin/overlay/images/` holds the splash, About and horizontal
258	     lockups, monochrome mark, wizard watermark, and window icons under
259	     OrcaSlicer's own asset names. `Slic3r::var()` checks that directory
260	     first, so no logo call site is edited. See the README there.
261	   - `Brand/brand_catalogs.py` builds `resources/i18n/<lang>/<app key>.mo`
262	     from upstream's `.po` files with the product name substituted, plus an
263	     English catalog for the source strings, so every language reads "JusPrin"
264	     without touching a string or macro in upstream code. Attribution strings
265	     in About are excluded by the script.
266	   - The generic printer profiles' plate texture,
267	     `resources/profiles/Custom/orcaslicer_bed_texture.svg`, is overwritten
268	     with the JusPrin lockup; the file name stays because five profiles
269	     reference it.
270	
271	`tests/brand/test_brand_tokens.cpp` fails the build if a token edit breaks the
272	contrast rules above or leaves a token in one mode without its counterpart in
273	the other. The same test guards the radius, spacing, and type scales: the
274	`dimension.radius`, `dimension.space`, and `typography.roles` tables must match
275	the values in this document exactly, `typography.code` must stay a single
276	12/16 role, every component radius must be one of the scale values, and every
277	button recipe must name a type role rather than a raw size.
278	
279	Known gaps, all deliberate: ImGui panels and canvas notifications keep the
280	teal accent; the first-run setup wizard (an OrcaSlicer HTML page) is
281	Orca-branded until JusPrin's own onboarding replaces it; the About dialog
282	links to the OrcaSlicer website; vendor printer profiles other than the
283	generic ones keep their own plate textures; dark mode and the Preview canvas
284	were not visually verified.
285	
286	## Design handoff requirements
287	
288	Every high-fidelity product frame must:
289	
290	1. Include paired light and dark versions using the same semantic token names.
291	2. State the mode, viewport, component variants, keyboard focus, and any deliberate exception.
292	3. Use DIP, native density, and the standard radius scale.
293	4. Use HarmonyOS Sans SC for product UI, and monospace only for code (Figma's Code style uses Roboto Mono as a stand-in for the system font).
294	5. Show normal, hover, pressed, disabled, focus, error, warning, and success states as applicable.
295	6. Test long filenames, localized labels, dense settings, empty states, and narrow windows.
296	7. Use the original logo and existing functional icon system.
297	8. Label and justify any value that is not in the token files.
298	
299	The POC decks, rendered examples, horizontal lockup PNG, and generation sources remain available for visual-reference work through [POC reference](poc-reference.md). They are not runtime dependencies.

1	# Fork stewardship
2	
3	**Status:** Required discipline for every change to an upstream-owned file on `jusprin-newui`.
4	
5	JusPrin is a long-lived fork. Every line it changes in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line it re-resolves at every rebase, forever, by a person who was not there when the line was written. The rules below exist to keep that permanent cost small and, where it cannot be small, to keep it visible.
6	
7	One question generates all of them: **after this change, what does the fork own?**
8	
9	- Owning *product policy* is safe. It is ours, upstream will never write it, and it lives in our files.
10	- Owning a *small neutral seam* is acceptable. It is the kind of thing upstream might plausibly have written itself, so it survives refactors and could be contributed back.
11	- Owning *upstream's behavior* is the expensive kind. It commits us to re-deriving upstream's intent forever, and the day we take ownership is usually the day the behavior quietly diverges.
12	
13	Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Git merges text, not meaning: it conflicts when two sides touch the same or adjacent lines, and it stays silent when they touch different lines even if the result is nonsense. And a conflict is a *stop* — a human is forced to look — while silent divergence is unbounded and invisible. Conflicts are therefore not the enemy. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.
14	
15	## The ten principles
16	
17	### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much
18	
19	**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.
20	
21	**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. New files have probability zero, so their size is free; one line inside a function upstream is actively reworking is expensive.
22	
23	**The test.** How many separate places does this change touch, and how busy is each one? Would one seam deliver the same capability?
24	
25	**Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.
26	
27	### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge
28	
29	**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.
30	
31	**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.
32	
33	**The test.** If upstream restructures the code around this hunk, do I get a conflict or silence? If silence, would any test catch it?
34	
35	**Violation.** Moving a member out of a constructor's initializer list because a callback can fire mid-construction. Nothing in upstream's code records that invariant, so a future cleanup restores the old form with no conflict and no error.
36	
37	### 3. Add to upstream's code; do not revise it
38	
39	**Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.
40	
41	**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. A rewritten function fails badly: every future upstream change to it is a conflict whose resolution requires re-deriving two intents at once, in code no longer shared with upstream. Rewriting subtle logic also tends to change it, and you find out later.
42	
43	**The test.** Does upstream's line survive my change? If I deleted or replaced one, why could I not have added next to it?
44	
45	**Violation.** Replacing OrcaSlicer's undo and redo implementations with fork-owned equivalents in order to learn whether the history position moved. Re-expressing the vendor-specific snapshot walk silently dropped one of its branches. An additive helper that reports the result, leaving upstream's functions untouched, would have answered the same question.
46	
47	### 4. Own the policy; borrow the mechanism
48	
49	**Rule.** No product name, color, dimension, or product-specific decision in an upstream-owned file. Upstream files may gain small neutral capabilities; the policy that uses them lives in fork-owned code.
50	
51	**Mechanism.** Product specifics in upstream files are permanent divergence: they can never be upstreamed and never dropped, so they must be re-resolved forever. A neutral capability — a flag, a getter/setter pair, an event — reads like something upstream could have written, which is exactly why it survives refactors.
52	
53	**The test.** Would this addition look reasonable in an upstream pull request, with no explanation of our product?
54	
55	**Violation.** A product-named enum value inside a rendering class, or product decisions embedded in an upstream mouse handler. The fix is a neutral options struct plus a fork-owned controller that applies our policy.
56	
57	### 5. One seam beats many touch points
58	
59	**Rule.** Find the single place every path already passes through, and put the fork's line there.
60	
61	**Mechanism.** Each touch point is an independent conflict draw and an independent thing a future resolver must understand. Collapsing many small recurring costs into one is worth some indirection.
62	
63	**The test.** Do all the paths I am hooking already converge somewhere downstream? Is there one function that runs exactly when the thing I care about has happened?
64	
65	**Violation.** Publishing a history-changed event from undo, from redo, and from both history-navigation entry points, when all four funnel through a single update function that runs only on a successful move.
66	
67	### 6. One shared implementation is worth a guaranteed conflict
68	
69	**Rule.** When the alternative is two copies of the same behavior, keep the shared path and accept that it will conflict.
70	
71	**Mechanism.** A conflict is a stop; drift between two copies is silent and unbounded. Trading an invisible risk for a visible, small, recurring one is a good trade.
72	
73	**The test.** Where did the logic I removed actually go? A move has one implementation; only a duplication risks divergence. If I wrote new behavior beside an existing upstream path rather than calling it, upstream's future improvements will never reach our users.
74	
75	**Violation.** Writing a second object-duplication routine next to OrcaSlicer's clipboard path and pointing an existing dialog at it. Reusing the existing path — extending it where it was too narrow — keeps one implementation.
76	
77	### 7. Unavoidable conflicts must be easy to resolve correctly
78	
79	**Rule.** When you must delete or relocate an upstream line, say at the site what moved, where it went, and what a future rebase must carry across.
80	
81	**Mechanism.** The real cost of a conflict is not the stop; it is the chance of resolving it wrongly. Appending near an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — keep both — is right. Deleting an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — take mine, the logic moved — silently discards whatever upstream did to that line in the meantime.
82	
83	**The test.** Six months from now, is the natural resolution of the conflict I am creating the correct one? If not, what does the resolver need to read to get it right, and is that text next to the conflict?
84	
85	**Violation.** Removing an upstream snapshot label that upstream later localized. Git stops for a human, but the intent-faithful resolution throws the translation away, and nothing at the site says otherwise.
86	
87	### 8. Do not diverge where you gain nothing; converge where upstream already went
88	
89	**Rule.** No gratuitous formatting, reordering, or whitespace differences. Before reverting a cosmetic difference, compare against current upstream — it may have made the same change.
90	
91	**Mechanism.** Every valueless difference is a conflict site that buys nothing. And if upstream has independently arrived at your version, "fixing" it back creates divergence rather than removing it. Adopting a change upstream has already made converges the two trees early and makes the eventual conflict resolve itself.
92	
93	**The test.** Does this difference carry meaning? Has upstream already made it?
94	
95	**Violation.** Consuming a shared blank line in a list of build subdirectories, where upstream also appends entries.
96	
97	### 9. Verify the risk claim instead of reasoning about it
98	
99	**Rule.** Before asserting that a change is or is not rebase-risky, check it. Three checks, each one command: does git actually conflict there; has upstream already converged on the same change; is the change a move or a duplication.
100	
101	**Mechanism.** A coherent story about fork risk is not a true one, and every one of these is cheaper to check than to argue about. Reasoning alone reliably produces confident, wrong claims — that a lost change is "silent" when git stops for it, that a move is a "duplication," that a cosmetic difference is gratuitous when upstream shares it.
102	
103	**The test.** Did I run the simulation, or am I describing what I expect it to say?
104	
105	**Violation.** A report that lists which files are rebase-sensitive and calls the change narrow, without having run the merge simulation that would have found two lossy resolutions waiting in it.
106	
107	### 10. Pull direction dominates every local edit
108	
109	**Rule.** Replay the fork's own commits onto upstream. Never merge upstream in, and never rebase the whole branch.
110	
111	**Mechanism.** The fork's own footprint is small; the inherited release-branch history is not. Merging upstream in makes the conflict surface the entire divergence between the release branch and upstream's development line — none of it ours. Rebasing only our commits discards that inherited history by taking upstream's version of every file we never touched.
112	
113	**The test.** Am I replaying our commits onto upstream, or bringing upstream into ours?
114	
115	**Violation.** `git merge upstream/main`, which produces a conflict list dominated by vendor profiles, translations, and CI files that JusPrin has never edited.
116	
117	## Before you finish
118	
119	A change that touches upstream-owned files is not done until this is recorded in the handback or pull request:
120	
121	1. **The rebase simulation and its result.** Run it against current upstream and name both endpoint commits — measurements are not reproducible otherwise.
122	
123	   ```bash
124	   git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<fork base> upstream/main HEAD
125	   ```
126	
127	   For each conflicted file, state whether the natural resolution is correct or lossy. A lossy one is a defect to fix now, not a note for later.
128	
129	2. **An account of every upstream line deleted or rewritten.** Where the logic went, and why an additive form was not possible.
130	
131	3. **A statement of what the fork now owns.** Policy, a neutral seam, or upstream behavior. The third needs an explicit justification.
132	
133	An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It is not proof that a future rebase will merge, and never proof that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the focused contract tests, the full native build, the real multi-plate workflow, native gizmo input, and the stock-behavior regression checks.
134	
135	## This fork's terrain
136	
137	Facts specific to OrcaSlicer, worth knowing before choosing where to put a seam. They change over time; re-measure rather than trusting these.
138	
139	`Plater.cpp` is by far the busiest file the fork touches, followed by the central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt`, `GLCanvas3D.cpp`, and `PartPlate.cpp`. `GLToolbar` and `GLGizmosManager` are quiet. File-level churn is only a first approximation: some functions inside `Plater.cpp` have not been touched upstream in the entire life of this fork, and a seam there is far cheaper than the file's overall rate suggests. Measure the function, not just the file.
140	
141	Some native state is shared rather than owned by one object. OrcaSlicer's collapse toolbar belongs to `Plater` and is used by both the Prepare and Preview canvases, so a per-canvas guard cannot save and restore it correctly. Shared state needs one owner at the shared lifetime boundary, and exact restoration needs a getter as well as a setter.
142	
143	`MainFrame`'s Notebook is cheaper to wrap than to dismantle. Dozens of
144	upstream predicates — menu and shortcut enabling, `can_delete`, slice status
145	updates, undo/redo gating — key off `m_tabpanel->GetSelection()`, so removing
146	or reparenting the Prepare/Preview pages breaks them with no conflict and no
147	error. A shell gets a tabless full-window layout for free instead: hide the
148	strip via the public `GetBtnsListCtrl()` (wxBookCtrlBase gives a hidden
149	controller zero size, so pages fill the client area), and the stock slice and
150	print side buttons disappear with it because `ButtonsListCtrl` reparents them
151	into the strip at construction. The Phase 1 production shell reached a
152	19-added-line upstream footprint this way where the POC's reparenting shell
153	needed edits across eight upstream files.
154	
155	The same measurement gives the rule for every fork-owned screen that comes
156	after the shell. OrcaSlicer's surfaces (the stock homepage, Prepare, Preview,
157	Monitor, the settings tabs) stay inside the Notebook, because their
158	correctness depends on it. Fork-owned surfaces (the header, the Agent pane,
159	Home, and whatever follows) live outside it, as siblings of the Notebook in a
160	fork-owned sizer, shown and hidden by the shell. The shell *reads* the
161	Notebook's selection to decide what to show and *never edits its page list*:
162	no `RemovePage`, `InsertPage`, or reparenting of a stock page. Removing or
163	replacing a page hands the fork the meaning of that index. Upstream keeps
164	addressing it by number — `tpHome` as a dialog parent, the target of
165	`EVT_LOAD_URL`, the tab `post_init` returns to — and every one of those lands
166	on the fork's widget with no conflict and no error. If a fork surface truly
167	must be a page, append it last, where no upstream code addresses it.
168	
169	Navigation between screens stays a Notebook selection change even when the
170	screen being left is fork-owned. Menu and shortcut enabling, undo and redo
171	availability, and slice-status updates all read `GetSelection()`, so the
172	selection must remain the one record of which OrcaSlicer surface is active.
173	Showing Prepare any other way leaves those predicates answering for the wrong
174	page, silently.
175	
176	Some stock behavior is already exposed as an event idiom rather than a
177	function. Upstream itself drives plate slicing from two places with the same
178	sequence — the slice button and the Cmd+R shortcut both run
179	`plater->update(true, true)`, post `EVT_GLTOOLBAR_SLICE_PLATE` to the Plater,
180	and select the Preview tab — so fork code may repeat that short dispatch
181	without violating the shared-implementation rule; the behavior itself stays
182	owned by Plater's event handler.
183	
184	Historical measurements and the incidents behind several of these rules are in the [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) and, for the spike era, in the [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

Placement is not interchangeable, and each missing file has a silent signature — both documented in "Software GL on Windows machines without a GPU" in `agent-docs/jusprin/engineering-method.md` (on `jusprin-newui` since 2026-09-13, commit `318208608f`).
17	- Quick recall of the signatures: no `libgallium_wgl.dll` → `glcontext not ready, postpone init`, no `got opengl version`, black canvas all session. No `dxil.dll` → d3d12 initializes, then exit `0x80070057` on the first canvas draw with nothing logged. Both verified by removing the file and re-running. With all three present, both `d3d12` (default, `4.2 … D3D12`) and `GALLIUM_DRIVER=llvmpipe` (`4.6 … llvmpipe`) render.
18	- `slow_bootup` only moves the dxil crash from startup to first canvas paint; it is not a workaround.
19	- Lesson: a clear-only WGL smoke test passed under d3d12 because clearing compiles no shader, and was wrongly read as clearing the driver. A smoke test that skips the suspect code path proves nothing about it. (That test was removed from the repo for this reason.)
20	- A first-run datadir (e.g. copies of `C:\b\dd3`) logs ~630k lines in the first minute — the `GuideFrame::GetFilamentInfo` profile scan, driver-independent. Not a GL symptom.
21	- `D3D12 (Microsoft Basic Render Driver)` in the log is **Mesa's own d3d12 gallium driver on WARP**, not Microsoft's GLon12 mapping layer and not a real GPU. Confirm which GL is live by listing the process's loaded modules: the bundled Mesa shows `<exe dir>\mesa\opengl32.dll` + `libgallium_wgl.dll` (+ `DXIL.dll` once d3d12 has drawn), the unprovisioned fallback shows only `C:\Windows\SYSTEM32\OPENGL32.dll`.

1	# JusPrin production architecture
2	
3	**Status:** Selected architecture and production implementation boundary for `jusprin-newui`.
4	
5	JusPrin replaces OrcaSlicer's primary presentation and workflow, while retaining OrcaSlicer's mature manufacturing behavior. Product work must simplify how users express intent and verify a print; it must not fork slicing, geometry, rendering, picking, serialization, or history behavior.
6	
7	## Product composition
8	
9	The target project window has four stable regions:
10	
11	1. A compact machine and project status row.
12	2. A collapsible, thin plates and objects pane.
13	3. OrcaSlicer's existing Prepare or G-code Preview canvas.
14	4. A fixed Agent conversation and print-plan pane.
15	
16	The compact plates/objects pane is deferred to a later task. The first
17	production shell and Agent implementation must not depend on it; users interact
18	with objects through the native canvas and Agent until the pane is added.
19	
20	Prepare is the persistent workspace. **Check print** temporarily replaces its center canvas with Orca's real sliced Preview. **Print** opens Send preflight and never sends immediately. Project details are a drawer, and Monitor is a separate surface that can remain visible during other work.
21	
22	## Runtime architecture
23	
24	```text
25	OrcaSlicer process (C++17 / wxWidgets / OpenGL)
26	├── JusPrin application shell
27	│   ├── compact top navigation and machine status
28	│   ├── native plates/objects pane
29	│   ├── center workspace host
30	│   │   ├── existing GLCanvas3D Prepare canvas
31	│   │   └── existing G-code Preview canvas
32	│   └── wxWebView
33	│       └── local React/TypeScript Agent interface
34	├── typed workspace/controller boundary
35	├── existing Orca model, selection, plates, gizmos, and undo stack
36	└── existing slicing, project I/O, device, and print subsystems
37	```
38	
39	The boundary is deliberately conservative:
40	
41	- The viewport and overlays over the viewport remain native.
42	- The top row and object/plate pane start as native wxWidgets.
43	- C++ owns application and project state.
44	- The WebView receives versioned events and sends versioned commands.
45	- A WebView object pane may be evaluated later only as a contained presentation choice. It does not justify Electron or a WebGL viewport.
46	
47	## Authoritative ownership
48	
49	| Concern | Authoritative owner | JusPrin responsibility |
50	|---|---|---|
51	| Project model and object identity | Orca `Model` and `ObjectID` | Project a typed, session-scoped view |
52	| Plates and active plate | Orca `PartPlateList` | Present and request changes through commands |
53	| Selection and picking | Orca `Selection` and `GLCanvas3D` | Synchronize UI without feedback loops |
54	| Geometry transforms | Orca gizmos and `GizmoObjectManipulation` | Launch existing behavior and present exact values |
55	| Undo and redo | Orca undo stack | Expose availability and outcomes without a shadow stack |
56	| Slicing and Preview | Orca slicing actions and Preview canvas | Present Slice and Check print states |
57	| Project serialization | Orca 3MF and model serializers | Preserve compatibility; add migration only for new data |
58	| Agent conversation | React/TypeScript WebView | Render messages, write the words people and the model read, and submit typed commands (see [Where logic goes](#where-logic-goes-the-page-first)) |
59	| Agent print plan | C++/agent application boundary | Explain intent, decisions, uncertainty, and consequences |
60	
61	## Production integration boundaries
62	
63	### Shell host
64	
65	Use one fork-owned shell installed through one small `MainFrame` attachment. Startup policy belongs to a fork-owned bootstrap or shell factory, not to a growing collection of environment checks inside Orca constructors.
66	
67	The first production version may keep the legacy top bar, tab panel, Sidebar, and `GUI_ObjectList` constructed when existing Orca behavior depends on them. They should be excluded from the visible layout, not covered by a separate top-level window. Removing their construction is a separate lifecycle project.
68	
69	### Build registration
70	
71	Keep the explicit JusPrin source list in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/sources.cmake`. Orca's central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt` should contain one stable include rather than a growing list of fork-owned files.
72	
73	### Workspace boundary
74	
75	The production workspace API should retain the useful POC concepts: strong plate and object IDs, read-only snapshots, explicit command errors, typed change reasons, monotonic revisions, and move-only RAII subscriptions. Before production use it must also:
76	
77	- define GUI-thread requirements;
78	- define exactly when a revision advances;
79	- invalidate session IDs explicitly when a project is replaced;
80	- observe changes made outside the adapter;
81	- report history independently of widget visibility;
82	- report whether undo and redo actually changed authoritative state;
83	- avoid depending on `GUI_ObjectList` for model commands;
84	- provide plate selection, object import/addition, and other product-required commands;
85	- remain free of wxWidgets and Orca types in its public contract.
86	
87	When an operation is trapped in presentation code, expose the smallest behavior-oriented command from its current owner. Do not copy the operation into JusPrin and do not simulate input against hidden controls.
88	
89	### Canvas presentation
90	
91	Retain a product-neutral presentation API on `GLCanvas3D` and a fork-owned RAII controller that applies JusPrin policy and restores previous Orca state. Visibility and input must be independently controllable so invisible chrome cannot consume pointer events while active native gizmos remain usable.
92	
93	Production controls should be more granular than the POC's broad `render_overlays` switch. Independently classify the stock main toolbar, gizmo picker, active gizmo handles, plate actions, object labels, layer-editing controls, navigation aids, Preview legend, and Preview sliders. Shared controls such as Plater's collapse toolbar need one owner at the shell lifetime, not one guard per canvas.
94	
95	### Plates and objects pane (deferred)
96	
97	This pane remains part of the target product, but it is not part of the current
98	production-shell or Agent-WebView task and is not a prerequisite for either.
99	When it is scheduled, the production pane is intentionally smaller than
100	`GUI_ObjectList`.
101	
102	It must:
103	
104	- list and switch plates;
105	- list objects on the active plate;
106	- synchronize selection in both directions;
107	- add/import, rename, duplicate, and remove an object;
108	- expose less common operations through a selected-object menu, More, or the Agent;
109	- expand into a full tree only for multi-object, multi-part, multi-material, modifier, or print-order complexity.
110	
111	Every command must reuse Orca's snapshot, cancellation, plate-membership, selection, update, and serialization behavior.
112	
113	### Agent WebView
114	
115	The production Agent interface is a standalone local React/TypeScript package embedded in `wxWebView`. It requires:
116	
117	- a versioned command/event schema;
118	- deterministic mock conversations for UI tests;
119	- incremental message rendering and stable scroll anchoring;
120	- explicit keyboard, focus, shortcut, clipboard, selection, and IME rules;
121	- reload, startup, bridge-error, and unavailable-agent states;
122	- no direct ownership of Orca project state.
123	
124	#### Where logic goes: the page first
125	
126	When the same logic could live either in C++ or in a React page, put it in the page unless there is a strong reason for C++. The page is quicker to change (Vite hot reload instead of relinking a multi-gigabyte GUI library), its tests run in milliseconds under Vitest, and it is already where the words people read are written. The words the model reads belong there too.
127	
128	Strong reasons for C++:
129	
130	- **It reads or changes OrcaSlicer state:** presets, the model, plates, slicing, the device list. The page never owns project state (see the constraints below).
131	- **It is a limit or a boundary the app must guarantee:** what a tool accepts and refuses, which tools a session may call, what needs the person's approval, and what reaches the model provider (API keys, access codes, project data). Page code can state a limit; only the app can enforce it.
132	- **It has to work without a page:** the MCP server, background work, tests that run without a browser.
133	- **It depends on a thread or a lifetime the page does not have.**
134	
135	The printer panel is the example. The app sends the page facts only: sizes, spools, which printer is on a card, what a change changed. The page writes every word from them. It writes the model's instructions (`AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts`) and hands them over with `printer_instructions`. It writes the panel's own words, the opening line and the note that goes with each tap (`AgentUI/src/printerWords.ts`). The opening goes over with `printer_opening`, and a tap's note travels in the tap's payload.
136	
137	The app decides the tools -- the five printer tools and the four settings tools, the same in every mode -- checks every call, refuses one that does not fit the conversation (adding a printer outside an Add conversation, changing a printer other than the one it is about, a setting of anything but that printer), and refuses a turn that has no instructions rather than falling back to the project assistant's prompt. It posts the opening once per session, and a tap's note only when the tap goes through, bounded to 2 KB. It still writes the notes for what only it can find out when the tap arrives: the network printer has gone, its model id is not on the list, or a save or undo failed.
138	
139	Windows uses WebView2, macOS uses WKWebView, and Linux uses WebKitGTK. Local resource packaging must work on all three. The demonstrated prototype used a single-file local bundle to avoid WKWebView `file:` subresource failures; production keeps that approach, and CMake now produces the bundle from the TypeScript/React sources.
140	
141	MCP and broad agent autonomy are later layers. They must use the same typed boundary rather than changing viewport ownership.
142	
143	### Gizmo presentation
144	
145	Start with Move or Rotate and create one reusable native controller seam around existing behavior:
146	
147	1. Show a compact action strip in the Prepare canvas's upper-left corner: a horizontal row, the way OrcaSlicer's own toolbar runs, but justified left rather than centred. It does not follow the selection or the camera: a strip docked to the object jumps whenever the view orbits. `Canvas/ViewportToolStrip` draws it with ImGui inside the canvas's own frame, through `GLCanvas3D::set_overlay_renderer`, and reads the open tool from the gizmo manager every frame. The open tool's values hang below the row in `Canvas/ToolValuePanel`, aligned with the button that opened it.
148	2. Activate the existing native gizmo.
149	3. Preserve existing pointer manipulation, snapping, and selection.
150	4. Route exact numeric entry through `GizmoObjectManipulation`.
151	5. Preserve existing snapshot timing and undo/redo.
152	6. Dismiss without inventing a draft transaction; Undo remains the revert path unless product requirements explicitly change.
153	
154	Then convert tools by interaction family: Move/Rotate/Scale; Mirror/Duplicate/Place on face; Measure; Cut/Repair; Text/Emboss; painter-based tools.
155	
156	### Semantic annotations
157	
158	Reuse existing painter raycasting, brush selection, clipping, facet visualization, copying, undo, and 3MF persistence. The unproven production delta is arbitrary semantic labels and their agent-facing representation. The first implementation should use two labels on one object and verify save/reload, transforms, duplication, undo/redo, and behavior under topology changes before expanding the palette.
159	
160	## Non-negotiable constraints
161	
162	- Do not change slicing algorithms for UI convenience.
163	- Do not replace `GLCanvas3D` or G-code Preview.
164	- Do not reimplement geometry operations in TypeScript.
165	- Do not place WebView content over the native GL canvas.
166	- Do not create a JavaScript shadow project model or undo stack.
167	- Preserve 3MF projects, printer profiles, shortcuts, serialization, and cross-platform behavior.
168	- Do not seek stock Orca feature parity when the product definition does not require it.
169	- Do not reopen Electron or WebGL without a new explicit product decision backed by evidence.
170	
171	## Implementation order
172	
173	1. Establish canonical product documents, design tokens, and curated assets.
174	2. Productionize the workspace contract, canonical Orca commands, observation, and real-adapter tests.
175	3. Productionize the canvas presentation/controller seam.
176	4. Build the production shell without a compact object/plate pane.
177	5. Build the typed Agent WebView and bridge.
178	6. Add the Move/Rotate presentation controller and roll out gizmo families.
179	7. Add semantic annotations, Check print reporting, Send preflight, Monitor, calibration, and troubleshooting surfaces according to the product definition.
180	8. Add the compact object/plate pane as a separately planned task when it is prioritized.
181	
182	Historical implementations and detailed proof are intentionally not copied here. See [POC reference](poc-reference.md).
183

# Left pane: handback

Working notes for Kenneth, 2026-10-02. Untracked on purpose; nothing here is committed.

The plates and project pane is implemented on `claude/left-pane-implementation-handoff-d2959c` (base `38ac3e9e1a`, which is `origin/jusprin-newui`). Nothing is committed yet. No OrcaSlicer-owned file is touched, so there is no rebase evidence to record.

## What was built

| Area | Where |
| --- | --- |
| Rows and navigation, no GUI | `Shell/LeftPaneModel.{hpp,cpp}` |
| The pane and its painted rows | `Shell/LeftPane.{hpp,cpp}` |
| Layout, collapse, Home hiding, ledger fan-out | `Shell/ShellController.{hpp,cpp}` |
| Header menu loses the project entries | `Shell/StatusRow.{hpp,cpp}`, `Shell/ProjectErrors.hpp` |
| Per-copy flags, off-plate group, copy selection, four commands | `Workspace/Workspace.hpp`, `Workspace/OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.{hpp,cpp}` |
| Tokens and guards | `resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json`, `Shell/ShellTheme.{hpp,cpp}`, `tests/brand/test_brand_tokens.cpp`, `tests/jusprin/test_shell_theme.cpp` |
| Docs | `architecture.md` (pane section), `design-system.md` (two component entries) |

The four new workspace commands each go through the path OrcaSlicer's own UI uses:

| Command | OrcaSlicer path |
| --- | --- |
| `select_copy` | `Selection::add_instance`, then the canvas's `EVT_GLCANVAS_OBJECT_SELECT` |
| `select_plate` | `Plater::select_plate` |
| `add_plate` | the toolbar's `EVT_GLTOOLBAR_ADD_PLATE` |
| `show_selection` | `GLCanvas3D::zoom_to_selection` |

## Verification

All runs are from a private tree, `C:\b\lpn`, Release, on the Windows box at 200% display scaling.

| Suite | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `jusprin_tests` (includes the 11 new left-pane model cases) | 455 assertions pass |
| `brand_tokens_tests` | pass; the one `[!mayfail]` case fails as before |
| `shell_theme_tests` | 125 assertions pass |
| `workspace_contract_tests` (5 new cases) | 248 assertions pass |
| `agent_bridge_tests` | 5215 assertions pass |
| AgentUI / HomeUI `npm test` | 242 / 61 pass |
| `shell_integration_harness --left-pane`, light | 155 checks pass |
| `shell_integration_harness --left-pane`, dark | 155 checks pass |
| `shell_integration_harness --external-project-history` | 69 pass (restore now driven through the pane) |
| `shell_integration_harness --classic-switch` / `--stock` | 32 / 24 pass |
| `workspace_adapter_integration_harness` (28 new `pane_` checks) | 800 pass |
| `shell_integration_harness` default mode | 512 pass, 4 fail (pre-existing, below) |

The `--left-pane` scenario covers plate switching, object and copy selection in both directions, add plate with undo and redo, an excluded copy, OrcaSlicer's own Printable switch, an off-plate object, tab switching, every Project view, Back and Escape, a recorded print, collapse and expand, a narrow window, Home and back in both states, slicing and re-slicing, and project replacement.

By hand, with real pointer and key input in `--manual-left-pane`: a plate row click, hover, the focus ring, Up/Down between rows, Enter, Escape, a pick on the canvas, a click on empty canvas, and Collapse.

Not verified: 100% and 150% scaling (the RDP session has to be reconnected at those scales), macOS, and Linux.

### Pre-existing failures

- **Default shell mode, 4 checks:** `failed_autosave_is_visible`, `failed_autosave_has_plain_status_text`, `failed_autosave_blocks_project_release`, `earlier_model_version_available`. They fail the same way on a copy of the main checkout's harness build, which has none of this work. The test makes a directory read-only with POSIX permissions, which Windows ignores.
- **Real-adapter harness:** it aborted on Windows in `verify_reopened_local_versions` because the test kept `HEAD` and `current-state.json` open while the store replaced them. I closed the streams in the test (3 lines). It had also never had its runtime DLLs copied beside it; it runs with the shell harness's Release folder on `PATH`.

## Where the implementation differs from Figma or the handoff

Decisions for you:

result.output:
Decisions for you:

1. **Add model.** Figma has **+ Add model** in both Plates frames; the handoff says import stays in its existing homes. I included the button and wired it to OrcaSlicer's own Add action (`Plater::add_file`). Removing it is one `set_add_model` call in `ShellController`.
2. **Preview.** The pane is shown on Prepare only. In Preview OrcaSlicer still draws its own plate picker, and two plate lists side by side looked wrong.
3. **`status.successSubtle`.** The "Sliced" chip's ground, `#E8F5EE`, had no token. I added it with a dark value of my own, `#1D3229` (5.65:1 under the dark success text). The dark value needs your sign-off.
4. **Narrow windows.** Below about 850 DIP wide with both panes open, the canvas falls under its 320 DIP minimum (318 DIP measured at an 860 DIP window). Nothing closes a pane on its own, as the handoff requires.

Recorded gaps:

- **Inactive plates' objects** use `text.tertiary` at full strength. Figma's 60% opacity measures 2.6:1.
- **The selected row's `visibility-toggle` dot** is not built; neither Figma nor the handoff says what it does.
- **`object-color-dot`** is a neutral bullet, not the object's filament colour.
- **Save state** reads "Saved", "Saving…" or "Couldn't save". Figma shows "Saved 14:02"; autosave does not expose a last-saved time.
- **Print history** shows the count and one line, "Details weren't recorded for these prints." Figma's "Future prints will appear here with date, plate, time, and filament" is left out because this version does not record them, and "older" is dropped because it implies newer prints have details.
- **Print records** are written by an Agent tool with defaulted times and slice-estimate statistics, so none are drawn as rows.
- **Version preview in the 3D view** does not exist today, so it is not built. Restore keeps its confirmation and its errors.
- **No Figma frame** exists for Details, Version history, the off-plate group, an excluded copy, the Empty and Slicing… chips, or dark mode. I drew them from the same rows and tokens.
- **Collapse** appears only in the one-plate frame; I applied that chrome to every state.
- **The pane has no resize handle**; Figma fixes it at 200.
- **Keyboard:** Up and Down move between the pane's rows. Tab stays OrcaSlicer's Prepare/Preview switch.
- **After a restore** the Project tab returns to its list, because a restore replaces the project.

## Captures

- `pane-states-light-dark.png`: eight pane states, light over dark.
- `window-two-plates-light.png`, `window-two-plates-dark.png`, `window-collapsed-light.png`, `window-narrow-light.png`: the whole window at 1280x800 DIP (the Figma frame size), and at 900 DIP wide.

# Copy the Mesa software-GL set into a Windows build tree.
#
# A verification machine with no GPU reports system GL 1.1, so OrcaSlicer's
# launcher loads "<exe dir>\mesa\opengl32.dll" instead. Neither that stub nor the
# libgallium_wgl.dll it imports is produced by CMake or checked in, so every
# freshly configured build tree needs this step or the 3D canvas stays black.
#
# Placement is not interchangeable: libgallium_wgl.dll must sit beside the
# executable (Windows resolves a dependent DLL against the process directory,
# not the importing DLL's), and opengl32.dll must sit in the mesa\ subfolder
# (the launcher loads it by that exact relative path). Swapping them either
# leaves the stub unresolvable or shadows the system GL and kills the app at
# launch. Harnesses are the exception: they have no launcher, so they also get
# a copy of opengl32.dll beside them.
#
# dxil.dll also goes beside the executable. Mesa's d3d12 driver, which it selects
# by default on WARP, needs it to sign the shaders it translates; without it the
# first shader-backed draw kills the process with 0x80070057. Windows Server does
# not ship it, but every Windows SDK does, so it is taken from the SDK by default.
#
# Failure signatures: "Software GL on Windows machines without a GPU" in
